#| include: false

# Step 1 lecture

## 1. What the package does

> 1. In Step 1, you have seen how to create a summary table and modify it for various statistical analyses. Summarize the package's capabilities as explained by the speaker. How may the {gtsummary} benefit you for your school work or career?

In Dr. Jung’s lecture, `tbl_summary()` puts counts and percentages for categorical variables and summaries such as the median and interquartile range for numeric variables in one table. The `by` argument makes it easy to compare groups side by side.

- `add_p()` adds the result of a group comparison. The lecture showed when to use tests such as Welch’s t-test, Wilcoxon rank-sum, and chi-square.
- `add_difference()` puts the size and uncertainty of a difference next to the group summaries. A p-value alone would leave me guessing about how large the difference actually was.
- `tbl_cross()` displays counts and percentages for two categorical variables. `tbl_regression()` organizes estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values from a fitted model.

::: {.notes}
Mention that Welch’s test compares means and Wilcoxon uses ranks. The choice depends on the question and the data.
:::

## How I would use it

For my RKR project, I could set up one table showing how single photos and carousels compare on reach, likes, and saves. If the team receives another export, I can rerun the same code with the same labels and definitions. That would save me from copying numbers into a new table every time the data changes.

. . .

For a marketing job, I would use the same approach to summarize campaign tests. I’d want a manager to see the sample size and the size of a difference before deciding whether it’s worth changing the content schedule.

# Extended presentation

## 2.1 Where each package fits

> 2. In Step 2, you watched the extended presentation of the {gtsummary} package by ***Dr. Daniel Dsjoberg***, the very creator of the package.
>
> 2.1. How does it differ from gt and gtExtras?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
**{gtsummary}**

Starts from data or a fitted model and organizes the statistics. I’d use it to build a cross-tab or display a model.
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
**{gt}**

Builds and formats a display table. Once I convert a summary with `as_gt()`, I can style the headers, add source notes, and adjust spacing.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**{gtExtras}**

Adds convenience functions to a `gt` table. A sparkline can show a trend inside a table cell if I have a time series for each row.
:::
::::

## 2.2 Three things to try {transition="fade"}

> 2.2. Give three things you learned newly that were not explained in the lecture in Step 1.

::: {.incremental}
1. **Pull a statistic into the write-up with `inline_text()`.** I can pull a coefficient or p-value from the same table used in the report. If I update the model, the number in the written interpretation can update too.
2. **Repeat the same summary across groups with `tbl_strata()`.** I could build the same format breakdown separately for standard and collaborative posts while keeping the table layout consistent.
3. **Choose a table output for the audience.** `as_gt()` was covered in Step 1. `as_flex_table()` gives me a route to an editable Word table when teammates need to revise a shared report.
:::

::: {.aside}
I used the package documentation to verify these three workflows. The assigned video is linked under References.
:::

# RKR Instagram data

## 3. Cross-tabulation

> 3. Apply what you learned to your MSDM CEP data. Choose two appropriate variables for cross-tabulation and show if the two variables are associated or not. Use appropriate statistics to test if the two variables are associated. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.

I used the Collins College post-performance export covering April 1 to October 1, 2026. I kept the 21 posts from the restaurant’s Instagram account, @rkr_cpp. The export contains single photos and carousels for that account.

I compared **post format** with **whether the post received at least one save**. Saves are one way to see which posts people may want to come back to. All 21 posts had a recorded save count.

## 3. Cross-tabulation code {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_export
#| output: false
library(gtsummary)

# cep_csv points to the original Collins College export.
raw <- read.csv(cep_csv, check.names = FALSE)
ig <- subset(raw, Network == "Instagram" & Profile == "rkr_cpp")
ig$format <- factor(
  ig[["Content Type"]],
  levels = c("Photo", "Carousel"), labels = c("Single photo", "Carousel")
)
ig$saved <- factor(
  ifelse(ig$Saves >= 1, "At least one save", "Zero saves"),
  levels = c("Zero saves", "At least one save")
)

save_table <- tbl_cross(
  ig, row = format, col = saved, percent = "row",
  label = list(format ~ "Post format", saved ~ "Save activity"),
  missing = "no"
) |>
  add_p(test = "fisher.test", pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3))
save_table

# Check that the small expected counts justify an exact test.
save_counts <- with(ig, table(format, saved))
outer(rowSums(save_counts), colSums(save_counts)) / sum(save_counts)
fisher.test(save_counts)
```

## 3. Cross-tabulation results

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (has_export) {
  print(as_kable(save_table, format = "pipe"))
} else {
  cat("\n", r"(
| Post format | Zero saves | At least one save | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Single photo | 0 (0.0%) | 4 (100.0%) | 4 |
| Carousel | 9 (52.9%) | 8 (47.1%) | 17 |
| All posts | 9 (42.9%) | 12 (57.1%) | 21 |
)", "\n")
}
```

Percentages are within each row. The expected counts for the photo row under independence were 1.71 and 2.29, so I used a two-sided Fisher’s exact test.

::: {.fragment}
All four single photos received at least one save, compared with eight of 17 carousels. **Fisher’s exact p = 0.104**, so the sample gives insufficient evidence of an association at the 0.05 level. With only four photos, I would treat the difference as a pattern to check in future posts.
:::

# Multiple regression

## 4. Regression setup

> 4. Using the MSDM CEP data, run multiple regression. The dependent variable can be continuous or dichotomous. Regress a dependent variable on a set of independent variables. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.

I used multiple linear regression to look at how **post format** and **collaboration status** relate to **engagement rate by reach**. The model helps me compare photo and carousel posts at the same collaboration status.

- **Outcome** is `100 × (likes + comments + shares + saves) / reach`.[^rate]
- **Predictors** are carousel versus single photo and collaborative versus standard. I grouped the export’s *Authored* and *Joined* categories as collaborative.
- **Sample** is 19 posts with recorded positive reach and all four interaction counts. Two carousels lacked reach.

[^rate]: Reach is the denominator in the CEP definition. The export also contains a separate impression-based rate.

## 4. Regression code {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_export
#| output: false
ig$reach_count <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", ig$Reach, fixed = TRUE))
ig$collaboration <- factor(
  ifelse(ig[["Collaboration Type"]] %in% c("Authored", "Joined"),
         "Collaborative", "Standard"),
  levels = c("Standard", "Collaborative")
)
complete_posts <- subset(
  ig, is.finite(reach_count) & reach_count > 0 &
    complete.cases(Likes, Comments, Shares, Saves, format, collaboration)
)
complete_posts$engagement_rate <- with(
  complete_posts, 100 * (Likes + Comments + Shares + Saves) / reach_count
)

model <- lm(engagement_rate ~ format + collaboration, data = complete_posts)
model_table <- tbl_regression(
  model, intercept = TRUE,
  label = list(format ~ "Post format", collaboration ~ "Collaboration status"),
  estimate_fun = label_style_number(digits = 2),
  pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3)
)
model_table

summary(model)
confint(model)

# Check how sensitive the estimates are to the most influential post.
most_influential <- which.max(cooks.distance(model))
sensitivity_model <- update(model, data = complete_posts[-most_influential, ])
coef(sensitivity_model)
```

## 4. Regression results

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (has_export) {
  print(as_kable(model_table, format = "pipe"))
} else {
  cat("\n", r"(
| Model term | Estimate (pp) | 95% CI (pp) | p-value |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Intercept (standard single photo) | 4.85 | 1.65 to 8.05 | 0.005 |
| Carousel vs. single photo | +2.69 | −0.80 to 6.18 | 0.121 |
| Collaborative vs. standard | +3.94 | 0.71 to 7.17 | 0.020 |
)", "\n")
}
```

**19 posts · R² = 0.372.** The carousel estimate compares with a single photo. The collaborative estimate compares with a standard post. Estimates are in percentage points (pp). Confidence intervals and p-values are based on ordinary least squares.

- At the same collaboration status, carousels were estimated to have a **2.69-point higher** engagement rate than photos. The confidence interval spans zero.
- At the same format, collaborative posts were estimated to have a **3.94-point higher** engagement rate than standard posts. The interval is wide and the estimate is observational.

::: {.notes}
The intercept estimates the engagement rate for a standard photo, which is the reference category for both predictors.
:::

## What I would tell RKR

Single photos had a higher share of posts with a save, while carousels had a positive estimated difference in overall engagement rate. These measure different things. A post can pick up likes, comments, or shares even when it gets zero saves.

The format estimate was sensitive to one post. Dropping the post with the largest Cook’s distance changed the carousel estimate from **+2.69 to +0.20 percentage points**. I’d keep both formats in the next round and compare them across similar topics and collaboration arrangements before using the result to change the content mix.

::: {.aside}
This analysis covers one account and one export window. Topic and posting date could also affect engagement.
:::
